storyTemplate.title: Horizon University
storyTemplate.description: Start freshman year at a normal American university after a rare late-blooming superpower wakes up days before move-in. Choose the power, manage college life, and decide who gets to shape your future.

story_source.title: Horizon University
story_source.description: Original superpower college story about a rare late-blooming freshman choosing a power and navigating Horizon University.

Lina Park.name: Lina Park

items.title: Choose Your Power
items.summary: Define the powerful late-blooming ability that manifested a few days before move-in.
items.completion_criteria: Completed immediately by EmberAdventures when the player selects one power option.
items.completion_instruction: Apply the chosen power rule and keep the scene at Alder Hall check-in. The player has arrived with this power newly awakened and not yet publicly understood.

rewards.text: The player has the power Null Presence. Null Presence can be turned on or off only by the player's explicit intent. The narrator must treat it as off unless the player clearly says they activate, use, turn on, or maintain Null Presence. The narrator must treat it as on until the player clearly says they deactivate, stop using, drop, or turn off Null Presence. When Null Presence is on, the player cannot be perceived by other characters in any way. This is not invisibility. Sight, sound, smell, touch, heat, air movement, footprints, displaced objects, cameras, sensors, instincts, and social intuition all fail to identify the player or the player's actions as caused by anyone. Characters do not say "who's there," do not investigate the player, do not notice being touched by the player, do not notice the player moving objects, and do not react to the player's body occupying space. If the player bumps, grabs, attacks, steals, opens doors, or moves things, nearby characters rationalize the event as normal, accidental, environmental, or continue their business without connecting it to a hidden person. The player still physically affects the world, but other characters cannot perceive the player as present while Null Presence is on.

The player has the power Wizard. The player can conjure elemental effects by clearly imagining the desired result and speaking a word or short phrase that describes the effect. The spoken phrase defines the effect: examples include "Fireball," "Ice Wall," "Gust," "Spark," "Stone Hand," "Mist Veil," or similar elemental phrases. The narrator should interpret the phrase directly and resolve a matching elemental manifestation. This power controls elemental forces such as fire, water, ice, wind, stone, lightning, mist, heat, cold, and light. It does not grant unrelated mind control, healing, teleportation, time control, resurrection, or reality rewriting unless the story later explicitly adds those abilities.

The player has the power Time Dilation. By explicit intent, the player can make the entire surrounding world appear to move in slow motion while they continue thinking, reacting, and moving at normal subjective speed. To everyone else, the player appears to move impossibly fast, precise, and reactive. Time Dilation affects the player's personal relationship to time, not a small local field: the whole world seems slowed from the player's perspective. It does not stop time completely, rewind time, travel through time, age objects, freeze selected targets, or alter past events.

The player has the power Singularity. By explicit intent, the player can manipulate gravity. They can make people, objects, or themselves heavier, lighter, pinned down, lifted, pulled inward, pushed away, crushed, or enhanced by gravitational force. The strength and area of the effect are determined by the player's intent and emotional state. Greater force, larger affected areas, or more complex uses require greater exertion and create more severe consequences, but the power is not limited to small-scale effects. If the player spirals into overwhelming rage, panic, hatred, grief, or desperation, Singularity may intensify dramatically and expand outward from the player, potentially affecting rooms, buildings, campuses, districts, or an entire city if the scene supports that escalation. The narrator should respect the player's declared scale and emotional intensity, showing appropriate strain, destruction, fear, injury, death, collateral damage, and aftermath. This power controls gravity only. It does not create portals, teleportation, time travel, matter creation, or general telekinesis unless the story later explicitly adds those abilities.

The player has the power Alchemist. By explicit intent, the player can convert matter into other forms of matter while respecting conservation of mass, matter, and energy. The player can reshape, refine, combine, separate, or chemically transform available material, but the needed matter and energy must come from the surrounding environment, carried materials, or the target itself. The narrator should allow clever uses such as turning carried metal into a sword, converting wood into gold, separating toxins from water, turning dense material into gas to cause pressure or explosions, or condensing gases from the air into a solid object. Large, dense, volatile, or energetically extreme transformations create matching consequences such as heat, cold, pressure changes, vacuum, wind, shockwaves, missing source material, chemical hazards, structural damage, or explosions. This power changes matter; it does not create mass from nothing, ignore energy costs, heal living minds, grant life, teleport objects, or violate conservation unless the story later explicitly adds that ability.

The player has the power Berserker. The player has extreme physical strength, enhanced speed, brutal endurance, and extreme regeneration without needing to transform or change body shape. They can strike, lift, throw, sprint, leap, tear, break, and survive at a level far beyond ordinary humans. Injuries heal rapidly, including wounds that would disable or kill a normal person, though pain, exhaustion, and emotional shock can still matter narratively. The narrator should allow direct physical uses such as smashing through barriers, overpowering attackers, catching or throwing heavy objects, sprinting faster than normal people can react, leaping across gaps, and recovering from severe damage. The power does not require rage to activate, but anger, fear, desperation, or protective instinct can make the player fight more violently and push harder. This power enhances the player's body only. It does not grant flight, ranged energy attacks, mind control, matter manipulation, invisibility, or immunity to all consequences unless the story later explicitly adds those abilities.

The player has the power Command Voice. By speaking clearly with intent, the player can lace words with supernatural authority that makes listeners feel compelled to obey simple direct commands. It works best on clear instructions such as "Stop," "Drop it," "Tell me the truth," "Walk away," or "Let me pass." The narrator should treat successful uses as powerful social and tactical pressure, while preserving that commands are spoken instructions rather than full mind control. This power influences obedience to direct commands; it does not rewrite memories, create love, grant loyalty, control absent people, force complex long-term plans, or remove all consequences from coercion.

The player has the power Deep Read. By explicit intent, the player can read hidden emotional, mental, and historical impressions from people, objects, or places. When focusing on a person, the player can sense surface emotions, strong intentions, lies, fear, attraction, guilt, hostility, and emotionally charged secrets. When focusing on an object or place, the player can sense recent emotional residue, important past events, who handled it, what happened nearby, or why it matters. The narrator should provide useful but scene-appropriate insight instead of vague nothingness when the player uses Deep Read. This power reads impressions and truth-patterns; it does not directly control minds, force obedience, alter memories, see the entire future, or reveal every possible secret unless the story later explicitly adds that ability.

story_rules.text: Horizon University is a normal American university first: dorms, classes, clubs, dining halls, parties, grades, policies, and friendships matter alongside powers.
Roughly half of people have powers, but most powers are minor. High-tier powers like the player's chosen power are rare, valuable, and dangerous.
Until the opening choice objective resolves, do not assume which power the player has. After the choice, follow the chosen power rule exactly.

world_notes: Most powered people manifest between grade school and middle school; high-school awakenings are late but known; college-age first manifestations are rare.
Civic Response is the official powered law-enforcement and emergency agency. It scouts powerful students for training and recruitment.
Criminal organizations recruit strong powers early with money, secrecy, favors, and protection.
unresolved_threads: Why did the player manifest so late and so strongly?
Who should define the player's future: friends, faculty, Civic Response, the underground, or the player?
rules_and_constraints: Keep the college grounded and recognizable; avoid turning it into a fantasy academy or powered academy.
Use hidden meters to steer attention without naming them in narration.

messages.speaker: Narrator
messages.text:
Move-in day at Horizon University smells like cardboard, hot pavement, laundry detergent, and cafeteria coffee.

You stand at the Alder Hall desk with a campus lanyard in your hand and a secret nobody here understands yet.

Most powered people manifest in grade school. Late bloomers usually happen in high school.

Your power woke up a few days ago.
